749	                                       5.2. Threats to Validity
750	                                            The protocol is duplicate-controlled rather than provably leakage-free. Exact dupli-
751	                                       cates and token- and AST-level clone families are removed, and the released folds share no
752	                                       hash, clone family or plugin, but semantic clones that differ lexically and structurally may
753	                                       persist. Collapsing clone families also changes the class balance, most sharply in Variant
754	                                       A, where the majority class becomes the vulnerable class; accuracy is therefore not compa-
755	                                       rable with the earlier release and macro-F1, balanced accuracy and MCC should be used
756	                                       for comparison.
757	                                            The dataset is incomplete: about 54% of indexed CVEs were unrecoverable because
758	                                       pre-fix releases and old SVN tags were pruned, so the corpus may be biased toward plugins
759	                                       that retain historical versions. Rare-class estimates are unreliable—RCE has 848 records
760	                                       in Variant B and several models never predict it—so four-class results should be treated
761	                                       as indicative. The neural models were trained on at most 4000 records per fold for 40
762	                                       epochs under a CPU budget, so their numbers are a lower bound; the test folds, however,
763	                                       are always complete. A transformer comparison is absent: the transformers library is not
764	                                       installed in the evaluation environment and the host has no GPU, so CodeBERT was not
765	                                       run and is not reported. A 256-token sensitivity run for the sequence models is likewise
766	                                       outstanding. Finally, the taint analyzer is intra-procedural and lexical, so its low recall
767	                                       reflects that implementation rather than taint analysis in general.
768	
769	                                       6. Limitations and Future Work
770	                                             The central limitation is that the labels themselves are only about half correct on the
771	                                       positive class, which bounds what any model trained on them can demonstrate. The priority
772	                                       is therefore data rather than architecture. First, expert-verified data at scale: extending the
773	                                       400-function review to several thousand functions with at least two annotators, adjudication
774	                                       and reported agreement, and evaluating on a genuinely expert-verified test set. Second,
775	                                       curated vulnerability feeds the supply entry point and sink explicitly, reducing reliance on
776	                                       diff heuristics. Third, semantic clone detection beyond token and AST similarity, since the
777	                                       present analysis removes only lexical and structural duplicates. Fourth, the outstanding
778	                                       runs: a fully resourced transformer comparison on identical folds and the 256-token
779	                                       sensitivity analysis. Fifth, given that a single-feature length baseline is competitive, future
780	                                       detectors in this domain should be required to clear such trivial baselines before semantic
781	                                       detection is claimed.
782	
783	                                       7. Conclusions
784	                                             We presented a duplicate-controlled benchmark of real WordPress plugin vulnerabil-
785	                                       ities and re-evaluated ten detectors on it. An audit of our own first release showed that
786	                                       plugin-level grouping does not prevent exact code duplicates from crossing fold boundaries,
787	                                       that identical code sometimes carries contradictory labels, and that a stacking ensemble
788	                                       described as out-of-fold was trained in sample. After correcting all three, the corpora
789	                                       contain 15,294 and 24,917 records with verified zero overlap across folds.
790	                                             On these corpora the best macro-F1 is 0.563 and 0.601 in the binary settings. No neural
791	                                       configuration leads in any of the six settings, a single-feature function-length classifier
792	                                       matches or exceeds the TF-IDF Random Forest in four of six, the source/sink rule has
793	                                       essentially no standalone detection ability, and the static analyzer misses about 98% of
794	                                       vulnerabilities. In-sample stacking is optimistic by 1.27 percentage points on average.
795	                                       Expert review finds 48.8% of the cleaned positive labels to be genuine.

28	## 1. Research objective
29	[A] To benchmark open-weight against frontier LLMs on function-level vulnerability detection, treating monetary cost and energy as "first-class axes alongside detection quality" (p. 1). The study also calibrates the LLM results against non-LLM reference points (static analysers and learned detectors) "to gauge absolute difficulty" (p. 2). [A] The authors claim the conjunction is new (a security task, a five-model open roster, and cost and energy as per-task axes), "not ... a priority" on any single axis (p. 3).
30	
31	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
32	- [V] No numbered RQs. Contributions are framed as (p. 2):
33	  - a cost- and energy-aware open-vs-frontier benchmark on label-clean PrimeVul with non-LLM reference points;
34	  - evidence on the quality–efficiency Pareto frontier;
35	  - an account of what can and cannot be measured for closed API models.
36	- [I] Implicit questions:
37	  1. Are open-weight LLMs competitive with frontier LLMs in quality?
38	  2. Are they more cost- and energy-efficient?
39	  3. How do LLMs compare with SAST and fine-tuned detectors at realistic prevalence?
40	
41	## 3. Methodology
42	- Research design: [V] Empirical benchmark of binary function-level detection ("does this C/C++ function contain a vulnerability?") on a fixed stratified PrimeVul sample (p. 4). Additional analyses (pp. 9–20):
43	  - re-scoring at the natural 1:44 prevalence;
44	  - configuration-matched families A/B/C;
45	  - prompt, sample-draw and run-to-run robustness;
46	  - a reasoning-vs-direct replication across two measurement epochs.
47	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Eight LLMs prompted zero-shot through a unified OpenAI-compatible API gateway (p. 4, Table 2). [V] The gateway is **not named** (pp. 4, 29).
48	  - **Frontier:** Claude Sonnet 5, GPT-5.1, Gemini 3.1 Pro (`gemini-3.1-pro-preview`); active parameters assumed ~100B for the energy estimate.
49	  - **Open-weight:** DeepSeek-V3.2 (~37B active), GLM-5 (~32B active), Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen3-Coder-30B (3B active MoE), Gemma-3-4B.
50	  - [V] Pinned providers and precision: DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 at GMICloud FP8; Llama-3.3-70B at DeepInfra FP8; Qwen3-Coder-30B at SiliconFlow FP8; Gemma-3-4B at DeepInfra bf16 (p. 29, Table A2).
51	  - [V] Main configuration: direct answer, reasoning disabled where permitted. Gemini cannot disable reasoning (HTTP 400) (p. 4, p. 29).
52	  - [V] Prompt: a security-reviewer persona; answer YES/NO first, then an optional explanation (p. 28). A lenient parser counts unparseable outputs as parse failures, not "safe" (p. 4, p. 29).
53	- Baselines or comparison conditions:
54	  - [V] **Trivial baselines:** always-safe and always-vulnerable (p. 7, Table 4); always-flag at 1:44 prevalence (p. 8, Table 5).
55	  - [V] **SAST arm** (p. 6, p. 10, Table 7): Flawfinder 2.0.20 (lexical), Cppcheck 2.21 (flow-sensitive), Semgrep 1.175 with community C and security-audit rulesets (pattern plus intraprocedural taint). A function is flagged if any finding reaches a swept severity threshold.
56	  - [V] **DL arm:**
57	    - CodeBERT fine-tuned on Devign (off the shelf, cross-dataset, argmax, 512 tokens) (p. 6);
58	    - CodeBERT (125M) fine-tuned on PrimeVul's training split, with the threshold selected on the validation split (p. 10–11).
59	  - [V] **CodeQL was not run.** PrimeVul functions are isolated snippets with no build, so no CodeQL database can be built (p. 10–11).
60	
61	## 4. Dataset and sample
62	- Data source(s): [V] PrimeVul test split (C/C++): 24,788 functions after loading, 549 vulnerable — "a realistic 1:44 class ratio" (p. 4).
63	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] N = 1549 functions: all 549 vulnerable plus 1000 seeded-random safe functions (p. 4). [I] Prevalence in the evaluated sample is 35.4% (549/1549). This is **not** 50/50, although the text once calls it "balanced by construction" (p. 8). [V] The effective N per model is 1526–1549 because parse failures are excluded (p. 6).
64	- Sampling / selection method:
65	  - [V] Label-stratified sample fixed by seed (p. 4).
66	  - [V] Two further near-disjoint safe pools (<6% overlap) were drawn for robustness (p. 19).
67	  - [V] LLM inputs were truncated to 8000 characters. This affects 105/1549 functions and 87/549 (15.8%) of the vulnerable ones; non-LLM baselines see untruncated code (p. 4).
68	  - [V] All CVEs date from 2008–2022 and predate the models' training cutoffs (p. 24). [V] The PrimeVul training split contains no evaluated function or function body (up to whitespace) (p. 10, p. 25).
69	- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Released on Zenodo (doi 10.5281/zenodo.21391073): harness, configurations, sampled function IDs, price snapshot, energy sweep, baseline scores and aggregated results (p. 26). [V] PrimeVul is fetched from its original authors by script; the fine-tuned checkpoint is regenerable by script (p. 26).
70	
71	## 5. Experimental setup
72	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
73	  - [V] Harness and decoding: a test-driven harness with 82 automated tests; temperature 0, seed 12345, one generation per item; output budget 64 tokens in the matched configuration (256 for two frontier models in the first epoch) (p. 6, p. 29).
74	  - [V] Cost: computed from logged input/output tokens × list price at a pinned provider, with gateway fallbacks disabled (p. 5).
75	  - [V] Provider price dispersion: up to 14.4× for DeepSeek-V3.2 (USD 0.209–3.000 per million input tokens) (p. 5, Table 3).
76	  - [V] Energy (p. 5):
77	    - FLOP estimate E ≈ 2·N_active·T·ε for API-served models;
78	    - measured with the NVML energy counter on a dedicated NVIDIA H200 for locally servable open models (concurrency 1, idle-subtracted "active" energy);
79	    - plus a concurrency sweep c = 1/8/32/64 (p. 14, Table 9).
80	  - [V] Latency: client-side under concurrency 10, so it conflates queueing (p. 30).
81	  - [V] Statistics: stratified paired bootstrap of balanced-accuracy differences (20,000 resamples, seed 12,345) with Holm correction over a 9-comparison primary family and a 15-comparison strict family (p. 6, p. 28).
82	- Code availability: [V] The harness and configurations are released (p. 6, p. 26).
83	
84	## 6. Evaluation metrics
85	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
86	  - [V] **Balanced accuracy** is the primary metric, because accuracy is dominated by the always-safe classifier (0.646 accuracy, above every LLM) and both trivial classifiers score exactly 0.5 on it (p. 6).
87	  - [V] MCC and F1 are also reported (p. 6).
88	  - [V] Deployment metrics at 1:44 prevalence are derived from the prevalence-invariant TPR/FPR (p. 8, Table 5):
89	    - precision; false positives per true positive (FP/TP);
90	    - alerts and found vulnerabilities per 1000 functions;
91	    - **USD per true positive** and **kJ per true positive**.
92	  - [V] Elicited 0–100 confidence gives ROC-AUC where usable. VD-Score is declined because the coarse score grids cannot reach its 0.5% FPR point (p. 9–10).
93	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals):
94	  - [V] Paired bootstrap 95% CIs and Holm-adjusted p for open-vs-frontier gaps (p. 27, Table A1).
95	  - [V] Wilson-based 95% CIs on precision at deployment prevalence for the non-LLM baselines (p. 10, Table 7).
96	  - [V] Robustness: Spearman rank correlation across prompts and draws (p. 19, Table 13).
97	  - [V] Output-budget effects are tested with a paired bootstrap (p. 16, Table 10).
98	
99	## 7. Key findings
100	1. **Detection quality, first epoch** — [V] Balanced accuracy / F1 per model, direct mode, N = 1549 (p. 7, Table 4). [V] F1 range across LLMs is 0.405–0.615 vs always-vulnerable F1 0.523 (p. 7, Table 4).
101	
102	   | Model | Bal. acc. (95% CI) | F1 |
103	   |---|---|---|
104	   | DeepSeek-V3.2 | 0.676 (0.654–0.697) | 0.615 |
105	   | Gemma-3-4B | 0.653 | 0.590 |
106	   | GLM-5 | 0.637 | 0.596 |
107	   | Gemini-3.1-Pro | 0.623 | 0.591 |
108	   | GPT-5.1 | 0.617 | 0.560 |
109	   | Claude-Sonnet-5 | 0.616 | 0.582 |
110	   | Llama-3.3-70B | 0.604 | 0.578 |
111	   | Qwen3-Coder-30B | 0.511 | 0.405 |
112	
113	2. **Open vs frontier significance** — [V] DeepSeek-V3.2 significantly beats all three frontier models: +0.054 to +0.060 balanced accuracy, Holm p < 5×10⁻⁴ (p. 6, p. 27, Table A1).
114	   - [V] Gemma-3-4B beats Claude-Sonnet-5 (+0.037, Holm p = 0.032); the other top-open gaps are not significant (p. 7, p. 27).
115	   - [V] Qwen3-Coder-30B is indistinguishable from chance (MCC 0.022, CI −0.03 to 0.07) (p. 7).
116	3. **Budget-matched second epoch (Family A)** — [V] Balanced accuracy / MCC: DeepSeek-V3.2 0.711 / 0.403; GLM-5 0.669 / 0.352; Gemma-3-4B 0.653 / 0.297; Claude-Sonnet-5 0.653 / 0.321; GPT-5.1 0.615 / 0.225; Llama 0.609 / 0.267; Qwen 0.568 / 0.136; Gemini 0.606 / 0.252, on only the 54.2% of tasks it answered (p. 17, Table 11).
117	   - [V] Claude equals Gemma (+0.0003, p = 0.98) (p. 17).
118	   - [V] Absolute numbers shifted by up to 0.06 between epochs seven weeks apart ("service drift") (p. 7–8, p. 20).
119	4. **Reasoning mode** — [V] Reasoning helps every frontier model (Claude +0.032, GPT-5.1 +0.044, Gemini +0.096) but hurts DeepSeek-V3.2 (−0.133, p < 10⁻⁴) and does not help GLM-5 (−0.019, n.s.); it costs 4.5–12.1× more per task (p. 17–18, Table 12).
120	   - [V] Best observed: DeepSeek 0.711 (direct) vs Claude 0.685 and Gemini 0.680 (reasoning); DeepSeek vs Claude p = 0.081 (p. 17).
121	   - [V] Reasoning lowers DeepSeek's specificity from 0.52 to 0.37 (p. 20).
122	5. **Prompt sensitivity dominates** — [V] Two paraphrases move balanced accuracy by up to 0.088 and produce three different winners (DeepSeek 0.711, Claude 0.741, GLM-5 0.700); Spearman ρ vs anchor = 0.381 and 0.810 (p. 19–20, Table 13).
123	   - [V] Safe-pool redraws move scores ≤0.015 (ρ = 1.000) (p. 19).
124	   - [V] Temperature-0 verdict agreement is 88.3–100%; only Gemma is exactly reproducible (p. 19).
125	6. **SAST baselines on the same functions** (p. 7, p. 10, Table 4, Table 7) — balanced accuracy / recall / specificity / precision at 1:44:
126	   - [V] Flawfinder risk≥1: 0.589 / 0.271 / 0.907 / 6.20%; risk≥4: 0.523 / 0.055 / 0.992 / 13.40%.
127	   - [V] Cppcheck: 0.548–0.592 balanced accuracy; precision 2.46–3.77%.
128	   - [V] Semgrep severity≥INFO: 0.514 / 0.031 / 0.998 / 25.96% (CI 5.7–66.9%). It flags 19 of 1549 functions with 17 TP and 2 FP (p. 11).
129	   - [V] Flawfinder is "ahead of every LLM at every threshold" on deployment precision but finds almost nothing (p. 9, p. 23).
130	7. **Fine-tuned DL baseline beats every LLM** — [V] CodeBERT-PrimeVul (125M, validation-tuned threshold) reaches balanced accuracy 0.765, MCC 0.526, recall 0.709, specificity 0.821, precision 8.23% at 1:44 (CI 6.9–9.7) and ROC-AUC 0.845 (p. 10, Table 7; p. 10–11). [V] CodeBERT-Devign (cross-dataset) collapses to 0.518, flagging 97% of functions (p. 7, p. 23). [V] At argmax 0.5 the PrimeVul detector predicts all-safe because no score exceeds 0.372. The authors "nearly reported" this artefact as evidence that trained detectors are no better than LLMs (p. 11).
131	8. **Deployment at 1:44 prevalence** — [V] Every LLM's precision is 2.3–3.8% vs 2.21% for always-flag; FP/TP ranges from 25.6 (DeepSeek) to 41.9 (Qwen); models alert on 43–75% of functions (p. 8, Table 5). [A] "Neither is ready for independent use" (p. 9).
132	9. **Cost per task** — [V] USD/task, first epoch (p. 7, Table 4); SAST and CodeBERT-Devign cost ≈0:

                               Second, security evaluations lean heavily on proprietary frontier models. A recent
                          review of offensive-security LLM studies found that proprietary systems appeared in
                          nearly every publication, while open-weight models were used in roughly half [4]. Yet,
                          open-weight models are precisely what many security teams need. They allow on-premises
                          deployment for privacy, compliance, and data-residency reasons, without sending sensitive
                          source code to an external service [8].
                               This paper brings the two concerns together. We benchmark eight contemporary LLMs,
                          a spread of open-weight and frontier systems, on realistic vulnerability detection, reporting
                          cost and energy as first-class axes, with latency as a confounded secondary measure. We
                          also calibrate the LLM results against non-LLM reference points, a static analyzer, and a
                          learned detector to gauge absolute difficulty. Our contributions are as follows:
                          •    A cost- and energy-aware benchmark of open-weight versus frontier LLMs on the
                               label-clean PrimeVul dataset [1], with a reproducible, test-driven measurement harness
                               and non-LLM reference points (Section 3).
                          •    Empirical evidence that open-weight models occupy the quality and efficiency Pareto
                               frontier, from a 4-billion-parameter model at the efficiency end to a sparse mixture
                               of experts at the quality end, while no frontier model is Pareto-optimal. We separate
                               two claims of different strength. The efficiency advantage is configuration-invariant: it
                               holds in every configuration we tested and widens when the frontier models are al-
                               lowed their native reasoning mode (Section 4). The quality advantage is configuration-
                               specific: at a matched direct-answer budget, the best open model significantly beats
                               every frontier model, but granting the frontier its native reasoning mode raises the
                               strongest frontier system to statistical parity with it, at several times the cost. The de-
                               fensible summary is, therefore, a decisive efficiency advantage together with quality
                               competitiveness, not quality dominance.
                          •    A precise account of what can and cannot be measured for closed API models. We
                               measure cost and latency directly throughout, measure energy on-GPU for the two
                               locally servable open models, and provide a bounded, assumption-explicit FLOP
                               estimate of energy for the API-only models. The measured points are consistent with
                               that estimate to within roughly a factor of two (Sections 3 and 4.6).
                                We are explicit that these results are a first, deployment-realistic snapshot and that
                          quality in absolute terms is poor. At PrimeVul’s natural 1:44 prevalence, every model we
                          tested raises roughly twenty-six false alarms per true finding, so the comparison identifies
                          the least miscalibrated model rather than a usable one; Section 4.3 quantifies this before any
                          deployment reading is drawn from the rankings. Energy is measured directly for the two
                          locally servable open models and FLOP-estimated with a sensitivity range for the API-only
                          models. Section 5 details these limitations and the extensions they invite.

                          2. Related Work
                          2.1. LLMs for Vulnerability Detection
                               Benchmarks for LLM-based vulnerability detection have proliferated. Meta’s CyberSe-
                          cEval suite evaluates insecure-code generation and broader cyber-safety [3]. SecVulEval
                          provides a large, de-duplicated, CVE-grounded C/C++ set with statement-level labels [2].
                          Independent evaluations temper early optimism. Ullah et al. found that leading LLMs
                          cannot yet reliably identify or reason vulnerabilities [9]. Steenhoek et al. reported only
                          54.5% balanced accuracy for state-of-the-art models on this task [10], a picture our results
                          corroborate. A recurring and central concern is label quality. The C/C++ datasets under-
                          pinning this literature have grown successively larger and cleaner, from Devign [11] and
                          Big-Vul [12] to the de-duplicated DiverseVul [13]. Even so, many widely used sets carry
                          substantial label noise and cross-split duplication, which inflates reported performance


                                                                                  https://doi.org/10.3390/computers15090623

                          now reported by some security evaluations; energy is reported by none of them, and the
                          general-purpose benchmarks that do treat energy seriously [5,7,17,20] do not evaluate a
                          security detection task. Breadth of open-weight coverage is likewise uneven: the study
                          that reports cost most carefully evaluates only proprietary models. What is new here is the
                          conjunction—a security detection task, a five-model open-weight roster spanning 4B to
                          671B total parameters, and cost and energy reported as co-equal per-task axes, with energy
                          measured directly where the model can be self-hosted. We make no claim to be first on any
                          single one of these axes.

                          3. Materials and Methods
                          3.1. Task and Dataset
                                We use binary function-level vulnerability detection. Given a C/C++ function,
                          the model answers whether it contains a vulnerability. We draw from the PrimeVul test
                          split [1] (24,788 functions after loading, of which 549 are vulnerable, a realistic 1:44 class
                          ratio). Because the test split contains only 549 vulnerable functions, a label-stratified sample
                          balances at most to 1098. We, therefore, evaluate on a stratified sample of N = 1549 (all
                          549 vulnerable functions plus 1000 safe functions), fixed by seed for reproducibility. For the
                          LLMs, function inputs are truncated to a fixed budget of 8000 characters to bound cost. This
                          affects 6.8% of the sample (105 of 1549 functions), and because vulnerable functions are
                          longer on average, 15.8% of them (87 of 549) are truncated. Where the vulnerable statement
                          falls beyond the budget, truncation caps achievable recall independently of model quality,
                          so the absolute recall figures are conservative. The two non-LLM baselines (Section 3.4)
                          instead see the untruncated function; so, on long inputs, they are, if anything, advantaged
                          relative to the LLMs. Each model is prompted to answer with a verdict first, followed by
                          an optional explanation. A lenient parser extracts the verdict, and outputs that yield no
                          parseable verdict are recorded as parse failures rather than silently counted as “safe”.

                          3.2. Models
                               We evaluate eight models spanning parameter scale and provenance (Table 2). All are
                          served through a unified OpenAI-compatible API gateway. Frontier models are proprietary,
                          while open-weight models are publicly available and, in principle, self-hostable. Reasoning-
                          capable models are run in a direct-answer configuration where the provider permits it.
                          Gemini-3.1-Pro exposes no non-reasoning mode and is, therefore, run with reasoning
                          enabled; Claude-Sonnet-5 and GPT-5.1 are run with reasoning disabled.

                          Table 2. Evaluated models. Active-parameter counts for frontier models are bounded assumptions
                          used only for the energy estimate.

                           Model                                Tier                         Est. Active Params
                           Claude Sonnet 5                     frontier                       ∼100B (assumed)
                           GPT-5.1                             frontier                       ∼100B (assumed)
                           Gemini 3.1 Pro                      frontier                       ∼100B (assumed)
                           DeepSeek-V3.2                         open                           ∼37B active
                           GLM-5                                 open                           ∼32B active
                           Llama-3.3-70B                         open                               70B
                           Qwen3-Coder-30B                       open                         3B active (MoE)
                           Gemma-3-4B                            open                                4B

                          3.3. Measurement Methodology
                                We treat detection quality, cost, and energy as co-equal evaluation axes and also
                          report latency. Because the open-weight models here are also accessed through the API
                          gateway, cost and latency are measured identically across all models, giving a like-for-
                          like comparison.
                                One caveat matters enough to quantify rather than merely state. The cost figure is a
                          gateway list price, and list price is not a property of a model. We captured every provider
                          serving each evaluated model through the gateway at a single instant (Table 3). An open-
                          weight model is typically offered by four to fourteen independent operators whose input
                          prices differ by up to 14-fold—DeepSeek-V3.2 ranges from USD 0.209 to USD 3.00 per
                          million input tokens and Llama-3.3-70B from USD 0.100 to USD 1.04—so which price one
                          pays is a routing decision, not a measurement. Frontier prices vary too, by up to four-fold



                                                                                  https://doi.org/10.3390/computers15090623

=== [PDF page 5] ===

Computers 2026, 15, 623                                                                                               5 of 32



                          across resale channels, but there the underlying service is a single opaque one. The more
                          consequential difference is that open-weight providers also differ in numerics: the same

                          them by recall provides almost exactly the reverse ordering by precision. The LLMs sit
                          at one extreme, flagging 45–96% of functions at 2.3–3.8% precision. Cppcheck spans the
                          middle. Flawfinder and then Semgrep occupy the other: Semgrep flags 19 of 1549 functions,
                          catching 17 true positives for 2 false ones, which is 3.1% recall at an estimated 26.0%
                          precision at deployment prevalence. That point estimate rests on two false positives, and its
                          95% interval is accordingly enormous, [5.7%, 66.9%], though even its lower bound exceeds
                          the point estimate of every LLM.

                          A Task-Specific Detector Beats Every LLM We Tested
                                The fine-tuned CodeBERT breaks that frontier, and this is the most consequential
                          result of our revision. With its decision threshold selected on PrimeVul’s validation split
                          and applied unchanged to the evaluated functions, it reaches 0.765 balanced accuracy,
                          MCC 0.526, and 8.2% precision at deployment prevalence while still recovering 71% of
                          the vulnerable functions. Every one of those figures is better than the best LLM in our
                          roster: DeepSeek-V3.2 scores 0.676, MCC 0.344, and 3.8% precision. It is not a marginal
                          difference. On MCC, the threshold-invariant metric, the 125-million-parameter encoder
                          exceeds the best of eight general-purpose models by more than 50%, and it does so at
                          negligible inference cost on a single commodity GPU.
                                Two methodological points keep this honest. First, the threshold matters enormously
                          and must not be tuned on the evaluation set: sweeping the threshold on the evaluated func-
                          tions themselves would have reported 0.777, and we report 0.765 because the 0.777 figure
                          describes the best a threshold could have achieved rather than what the detector achieves.
                          The gap is small here (0.013), which tells us the threshold transfers between splits, but it
                          is the kind of optimism that is easy to publish accidentally. Second, and more impor-
                          tantly, our first attempt at this baseline produced 0.500 balanced accuracy with recall of
                          exactly zero, and we nearly reported it as evidence that trained detectors fare no better
                          than LLMs on PrimeVul. That was an artifact: under unweighted cross-entropy on a split
                          that is 2.77% positive, predicting “safe” everywhere is the optimum, and no score in the
                          model’s output ever exceeded 0.372, so an argmax decision rule could not have produced a
                          positive prediction whatever the model had learned. The ranking underneath was strong
                          all along (ROC-AUC 0.845). We record this because the failure mode is silent, produces a
                          plausible-looking number, and would have supported precisely the wrong conclusion.
                                The comparison does come with a condition, and it is the one that matters for practice.
                          The detector is trained on PrimeVul’s own training split and is, therefore, in-distribution,
                          while the LLMs are evaluated zero-shot. That is not an unfair comparison—it is the choice
                          an organization actually faces—but the two options have different prerequisites. A fine-
                          tuned detector requires several thousand labeled vulnerable functions from the target
                          distribution; an LLM requires none. Where such labels exist, our results say plainly that
                          a small task-specific model is the better and far cheaper instrument, and that the LLM
                          comparison in Section 4.2 is a comparison among LLMs rather than a search for the best
                          available detector. Where they do not, the LLM results stand on their own terms.
                                None of this makes the task solved. At deployment prevalence, the trained detector
                          still raises eleven false alarms per true finding, and its 8.2% precision, while more than
                          double the best LLM’s, is not a number any triage workflow absorbs unaided.

                          active-parameter count, so the frontier carbon figure and the roughly 40-fold ratio inherit
                          that assumption’s 10- to 150-fold sensitivity, and the ratio compares one estimate against
                          another, since Gemma-3-4B’s energy is estimated too. The absolute footprints are modest
                          in isolation, but the ratio is large and recurring, and it compounds with every re-scan of
                          an evolving codebase (though a cheaper per-task scan may also induce more scanning,
                          a rebound effect that bounds the aggregate saving). This is a concrete instance of the “Green
                          AI” argument [5,17,29] applied to a security workload. The result is not that open models
                          are uniformly superior, since Qwen3-Coder-30B is indistinguishable from chance, but that
                          the best open models dominate the frontier on both the quality and the efficiency axes.

                          5.2. Why the Benchmark Is Hard
                               No LLM exceeded 0.68 balanced accuracy, and none beat the trivial always-safe
                          classifier on raw accuracy, an important sanity check on this imbalanced set. Two non-LLM
                          reference points frame the difficulty (Table 4). A classical lexical static analyzer, Flawfinder,
                          reaches 0.589 balanced accuracy, below every LLM except the near-chance Qwen3-Coder-
                          30B. Because it flags conservatively (specificity 0.91), it is the only method here that beats
                          the always-safe baseline on raw accuracy (0.682 against 0.646) at essentially zero cost.

                              effect at full scale. Reasoning buys a significant +0.03 to +0.05 balanced accuracy at 2.5
                              to 7.6 times the cost, bringing the strongest frontier model to statistical parity with the
                              best open model (0.677 against 0.676, within the confidence interval). The comparison
                              is symmetric. Enabling reasoning on the two open models with reasoning modes
                              (DeepSeek-V3.2, GLM-5) helps neither, and it significantly lowers DeepSeek’s balanced
                              accuracy to 0.608, so the open models need no reasoning, and the top-of-table parity
                              holds both ways. Our main-run 256-token cap also understated Gemini-3.1-Pro, which
                              reaches 0.677 at a 4096-token budget. Because reasoning multiplies cost and energy, it
                              cannot change the efficiency ordering.
                          •   Decoding-budget asymmetry. Two frontier models (Claude-Sonnet-5, Gemini-3.1-Pro)
                              needed a larger output budget (256 against 64 tokens) to emit a verdict reliably in the
                              main run and are reported at that budget; Claude runs with reasoning disabled, while
                              Gemini-3.1-Pro exposes no direct mode and is therefore reasoning-only. Because they
                              are already the efficiency losers, their reported cost and energy gap is conservative.
                              GLM-5, which we initially ran at the larger budget, is re-run at the matched 64-token
                              budget with reasoning disabled and reported there. Its balanced accuracy is essentially
                              unchanged (0.637 against 0.647), which confirms the budget does not drive its result.
                              Section 4.7 addresses the asymmetry directly by reporting budget-matched, native,
                              and best-observed configurations side by side rather than defending any one of them
                              as fair; Gemini-3.1-Pro remains the one model that cannot be budget-matched at all,
                              and we report its failure rate instead of a score.
                          •   Latency under concurrency. The service-latency figures we report (Section 4) were
                              collected under concurrent load and conflate model speed with queueing. A con-
                              trolled single-request latency pass is future work, so we treat latency as a directional
                              observation rather than as a precise axis.
                          •   Training-data contamination. PrimeVul is built from public CVE-fixing commits. All
                              of them here are from 2008–2022, predating the models’ training cutoffs, and they may
                              appear in pretraining data. Binning the vulnerable functions by CVE year reveals a
                              modest memorization gradient. Recall on pre-2020 CVEs is 7–15 points higher than
                              on 2021–2022 CVEs for the better-balanced models (for example, GPT-5.1 0.88 against
                              0.73, and DeepSeek-V3.2 0.90 against 0.81), consistent with some memorization of
                              older, well-documented vulnerabilities. The gradient appears in both tiers, so it does
                              not obviously explain the open-versus-frontier gap, but it does suggest absolute scores
                              may be optimistic. A cleaner bound would restrict to post-cutoff CVEs or to PrimeVul’s
                              paired vulnerable and patched variants, which resist superficial memorization, and
                              is planned.
                          •   Sampling and generation variance. The headline table uses one stratified draw of
                              the 1000 safe functions, one prompt template, and one generation per item at temper-
                              ature 0. The paired bootstrap (Section 4.2) bounds only within-sample uncertainty.
                              Section 4.8 varies all three directly—two additional near-disjoint safe draws, two
                              prompt paraphrases, and repeated generations of the fixed positive set—which is the
                              appropriate test because the balanced-accuracy ranking is specificity-driven and the
                              middle of the table is closely spaced. What remains unbounded is variation across
                              datasets and task formulations, not across draws of this one.
                          •   Serving-layer dependence, tested rather than assumed. Open-weight models reached
                              through a gateway are served by many independent providers differing in price by
                              up to 14-fold and in numerics, the same weights being offered at FP4, FP8, bf16, and
                              fp16 by different operators (Table 3). We expected this to threaten the open-model
                              quality figures and tested it directly: Llama-3.3-70B run on three providers in one
                              epoch with identical prompt, sample and seed—two at FP8 from different operators,

                          •    Baselines. Alongside the trivial classifiers, we report four non-LLM detectors
                               (Section 4.4): Flawfinder, Cppcheck, Semgrep with security rulesets, and an off-the-
                               shelf CodeBERT-Devign classifier, the last of which we present as a cross-dataset
                               transfer reference point rather than as a competitive detector. A learned detector
                               fine-tuned directly on PrimeVul’s own training split, in the LineVul [30] family, is the
                               remaining gap; we verified that no evaluated function, and no evaluated function
                               body up to whitespace, occurs in that training split, so such a baseline can be trained
                               without leakage. CodeQL [31] cannot be applied: its C/C++ database construction
                               requires tracing a real build, which isolated PrimeVul functions do not admit. That
                               is a limitation of the function-level task formulation, and it applies to any whole-
                               program analyzer.
                          •    Scope. We report one dataset, one task formulation, and a balanced sample of 1549 func-
                               tions. Generalization to other languages, to statement-level localization, and to the realistic-
                               imbalance regime (via a scored metric such as VD-Score [1]) belongs to future work.

4.9. Reasoning Versus Direct Answering: Replication Across Epochs
                               Section 4.7 reports the reasoning comparison within a single epoch, which is the
                          version we rely on. We ran the same comparison seven weeks earlier, before the anchor
                          re-run revealed service drift, and report it here because it replicates the qualitative pattern
                          on independent data.
                               In that earlier epoch, reasoning raised balanced accuracy for every frontier model—Claude-
                          Sonnet-5 from 0.616 to 0.646 (p = 0.013), GPT-5.1 from 0.617 to 0.660 (p = 0.002),
                          and Gemini-3.1-Pro from a budget-limited 0.623 to 0.677—and helped neither open model,
                          significantly hurting DeepSeek-V3.2 (0.676 to 0.608, −0.067, p < 0.001) while leaving GLM-
                          5 unchanged within noise (−0.017, p = 0.08). The in-epoch measurement reproduces all
                          five signs and the two significance patterns, with a larger penalty for DeepSeek (−0.133)
                          and a slightly smaller gain for Claude.
                               The mechanism is visible in the confusion matrices and is the same in both epochs:
                          reasoning lowers DeepSeek’s specificity from 0.52 to 0.37, so a model that was already well
                          balanced begins to over-flag. Reasoning is not a free improvement. It helps systems whose
                          direct-mode calibration is poor, and degrades one whose calibration is already good.
                               That two independent measurement epochs, seven weeks and one provider-pinning
                          change apart, agree on every sign is the strongest evidence we have that the reasoning
                          result is a property of the models rather than of a particular measurement. The absolute
                          numbers differ by up to 0.06 between epochs, which is exactly why Section 4.7 draws its
                          conclusions from one epoch alone.

                          5. Discussion
                          5.1. Open-Weight Models on the Efficiency Frontier
                                The central result is that open-weight models occupy the quality and efficiency Pareto
                          frontier, and no frontier model is Pareto-optimal. That frontier is spanned by two open mod-
                          els: the 4-billion-parameter Gemma-3-4B at the low-cost, low-energy end, and the sparse
                          mixture-of-experts DeepSeek-V3.2 at the high-quality end. The two axes of that result
                          carry different weight, and we keep them apart. The efficiency advantage is configuration-

== tashenova2026real
3:status: ready
9:main_finding: Best binary macro-F1 0.563/0.601; neural models never lead; token-count baseline rivals TF-IDF RF; unnamed intra-procedural lexical taint analyser misses ~98%; 48.8% of cleaned positives genuine.
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | On 24,917 real WordPress PHP functions (Variant B binary, plugin-grouped, de-duplicated), best macro-F1 0.601 (nested stacking); Bi-LSTM 0.573, SVM 0.562; no neural model leads in any of 6 settings | 7, 8 | V | weak–moderate (single study, single seed, ≤48.8% label precision, overlapping CIs) |
| RQ1 | An in-house intra-procedural lexical taint analyser detects 1.7–1.8% of PHP vulnerabilities (FNR 0.982; macro-F1 0.366 vs majority 0.350; MCC 0.035); unnamed, unversioned intra-procedural lexical analyser | 5, 8, 9, 13 | V | weak for SAST in general (single bespoke tool) |
| RQ1 | No LLM or pre-trained transformer evaluated (CodeBERT not run: no GPU/transformers) | 13 | V | n/a (scope) |
| RQ2 | Plugin-grouped folds still had exact-duplicate groups spanning folds: 166 / 151 groups holding 1086 (A) / 676 (B) records (test-side share not reported; authors call them test copies, p. 10); 730/456 groups had contradictory labels; conflict removal + dedup + clone collapse cut the corpus by 50.4% / 19.3% (collapse alone 11,123 / 3714 records) | 4, 5 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | A one-feature token-count baseline matches or beats TF-IDF RF in 4/6 settings; on Variant B binary it scores 0.572 vs Bi-LSTM 0.573 and best neural (uni-LSTM) 0.578 | 8 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Expert review: only 48.8% of cleaned positive diff-derived labels are genuine (73.0% HIGH, 44.7% MEDIUM, 0.7% LOW; single annotator) | 11 | V | moderate (n=400, 1 annotator) |
| RQ2 | In-sample stacking inflates macro-F1 by +1.27 pp on average (range −1.62 to +2.95) | 10 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Re-scored vs trivial predictors: always-vulnerable macro-F1 ≈0.316 (B) / 0.427 (A, = majority); best detectors beat majority by +0.251 (B) / +0.136 (A) and always-vulnerable by +0.285 (B); MCC ≤0.203 (Variant B only; A not reported) | 5, 8 | I | moderate (our pooled calculation from Table 2 counts vs fold-mean scores) |
| RQ4 | PHP per-class F1 (Variant B 4-class): XSS up to 0.500, SQLi ≤0.146, RCE ≤0.085; RF never predicts RCE | 9 | V | weak (rare classes) |
| RQ5 | Authors: label quality, not architecture, is the binding constraint; detectors should be required to clear trivial baselines | 12, 13 | A | moderate |

|---|---|---|---|---|

## tashenova2026real · ready · full-text

**Findings applied (1–10 plus Minor):**
1. **main_finding** now names the tool as an "unnamed intra-procedural lexical taint analyser". §14 has an [I] scope note under the two "misses about 98%" quotes (p. 5, p. 13).

3. **"1086 / 676 test copies":** the authors' claim is now [A] (p. 10). The [V] fact is that Table 1 (p. 4) counts these as all records in duplicate groups that span folds. How many were on the test side is not reported. Changed in §7 #7 and the RQ2 row.
4. **§3 SAST bullet:** split into [V] "unnamed, no version" (p. 5, p. 13) and [I] "does not match an established tool / probably SentinelCMS".
5. **§7 #11 margins over trivial baselines:** +0.136 (A) and +0.251 (B) over majority, +0.285 (B) over always-vulnerable. MCC ≤ 0.203 is now marked as Variant B only; Variant A MCC is not reported. Added a caveat that the paper's scores are fold means while our baseline calculation is pooled. RQ2 [I] row updated.
6. **§6 statistics:** the fold-level test is unnamed and has no p-value. Only the plugin-level result (p = 0.295, d = 0.057) is quantified. Added an [I] note that an exact two-sided Wilcoxon test with n = 5 cannot go below p = 0.0625. The §9 presentation bullet now matches.
7. **Funding/COI:** new bullet in §10. [V] no external funding and no COI declared (p. 14). [I] this is a self-re-evaluation of the authors' own SentinelCMS (p. 2), but any bias runs against their own earlier claims.
8. **§7 #4:** split into an [A] quote and a [V] correction. The paper calls the Bi-LSTM (0.573) the "best neural model", but the uni-LSTM scores 0.578 in Table 5. Also noted that Table 4 gives the Bi-LSTM 0.572 and Table 5 gives 0.573 (p. 7, p. 8). RQ2 row updated.
9. **§12 G5:** stays open pending a novelty check against Neef et al. 2026 (arXiv:2606.21397). I verified that deininger cites it on p. 3 as covering "web vulnerability detection in WordPress plugins". Neither of us has read it.
10. **Strength:** RQ1 row 1 is now weak–moderate.

8. **PrimeVul test-split counts:** [I] note in §4 that 24,788 / 549 differs from the 695 / 25,216 in ding2025vulnerability, cited as [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 6]. The paper only says "after loading". I confirmed both numbers in ding's analysis and its fulltext.
9. **Triage:** "human triage not included" is now [I]. The paper only says "No triage workflow absorbs that" (p. 8).
10. **Author-stated limitations:** contamination (p. 24) and the in-distribution vs zero-shot asymmetry (p. 11) are now [A] in §8. §9 keeps only our [I] point that the two effects pull in opposite directions.
11. **§1 quote:** replaced with the verbatim "We make no claim to be first on any single one of these axes" (p. 3).
